_comment: ROUND 2 — the eight publishers from the experiment set that (a) publish no AI-crawler
restriction in robots.txt and (b) actually answered us. Not shipped config; nothing loads this
without --config.
DROPPED from round 1, and why:
Le Monde, FAZ, El Pais, Corriere, NZZ, FT, Al Jazeera, ABC Australia — block ClaudeBot and
anthropic-ai by name. Technically our user-agent is not on their lists; we are not going
to route around a published position on a technicality.
The Times of Israel — allows us in robots.txt, then answers 403. A refusal in the mechanism
that actually enforces outranks a permission in the one that does not.
CBC News — robots.txt timed out twice. The gate fails closed, so it is out until it can be
read; datacenter-IP blocking is the likely cause (NPR fails identically).
EVERY SITEMAP URL BELOW WAS HARVESTED FROM THE PUBLISHER'S OWN robots.txt in round 1 — none is
a guess. That was the point of running round 1 section-only: guessing eighteen sitemap paths
would have produced a table of 404s that said nothing about the publishers.
The sitemap rung leads and section is the fallback, because a section index states no
publication date. Round 1 returned 810 candidates with ZERO dated, so every one of them would
have ingested as missing metadata with no position in Latest and nothing for clustering to
order by. `dated` is now measured per publisher; that is the number this round exists to move.
The Japan Times declares no sitemap in robots.txt, so it stays section-only and is expected to
report 0% dated — the control case for exactly the problem above.
min_interval states the publisher's OWN Crawl-delay where they publish one: SCMP and The
Straits Times both ask for 10s. The crawler already honoured max(configured, declared) at
runtime, so this changes no behaviour — it stops the config from understating what we owe them.
